method_card.title: Cumulative Frequency, Box Plots & Histograms
steps: Cumulative frequency: add running totals, plot at upper class boundaries, join with a smooth curve.
Read the median at n ÷ 2, Q1 at n ÷ 4, Q3 at 3n ÷ 4. IQR = Q3 − Q1.
Box plot shows five values: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum.
Histogram: frequency density = frequency ÷ class width, so frequency = fd × width.
method_card.content:
Cumulative frequency (CF) is a running total, plotted against the upper class boundary. Read the median at \(n/2\), Q1 at \(n/4\), Q3 at \(3n/4\); then IQR = Q3 − Q1.

A box plot shows minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum. Histograms use frequency density = frequency ÷ class width, so frequency = fd × width.
method_card.example: 80 students. The median is at the \(80/2 = 40\)th value. Read across from a cumulative frequency of 40 to find the median score.

problem_bank.bronze_description: One-step reads: a median, quartile, IQR, range or frequency density straight from a graph, box plot or single class.
problem_bank.silver_description: Two-step work: frequency from density and width, totals across unequal bars, or two quartiles read off a curve.
problem_bank.gold_description: Multi-step estimates: split a class, subtract from the total, or turn a quartile into a percentage or count.

bronze.title: Bronze: reading a single value
steps: Cumulative frequency (CF) is a running total. On a CF graph the median is at position \(n/2\), the lower quartile \(Q_1\) at \(n/4\), the upper quartile \(Q_3\) at \(3n/4\): read up to that height, across to the curve, then down to the value.
A box plot shows five values in order: minimum, \(Q_1\), median, \(Q_3\), maximum. The IQR is \(Q_3 - Q_1\) and the range is maximum minus minimum.
For a single histogram class, frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.

example.question: A box plot has minimum 8, Q1 = 15, median 20, Q3 = 27, maximum 34. Find the IQR.

steps.label: Pick the quartiles
steps.content: IQR uses only the two box edges, \(Q_3\) and \(Q_1\), not the median.

steps.label: Check
steps.content: 27 and 15 are the quartiles, and \(27 - 15\) leaves a positive spread.

silver.title: Silver: two-step frequency and spread
steps: To turn a histogram bar into a real frequency, multiply: frequency = frequency density × class width. Watch the width: a class like 20 to 50 is 30 wide, not 10.
Add every bar's frequency to get the total. To go the other way, frequency density = frequency ÷ width.
On a CF graph, read \(Q_1\) at \(n/4\) and \(Q_3\) at \(3n/4\), then IQR = \(Q_3 - Q_1\).

example.question: A histogram has classes 0 to 10 (fd 3) and 10 to 40 (fd 2). Find the total frequency.

steps.label: Check
steps.content: The wider bar holds more, and \(60 > 30\) fits.

gold.title: Gold: multi-step estimates from graphs
steps: Some questions ask for part of a class. Find the whole bar's frequency (fd × width), then take the fraction you need, assuming the data is spread evenly across the class.
'More than \(x\)' from a CF graph means total − cumulative frequency at \(x\): read the CF at \(x\), then subtract from \(n\).
Above \(Q_3\) is the top 25%; between \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) is the middle 50%. Multiply the percentage by \(n\) for a count.

steps.label: Top quarter
steps.content: Above \(Q_3\) is the top 25% of the data.

steps.label: Check
steps.content: 25% of 160 is a quarter, and a quarter of 160 is a whole number.

opener.label: Before any graphs
opener.display:
A shop counts customers as the morning goes on:
By 9am: 4 customers
By 10am: 10 customers
By 11am: 20 customers

steps.hint: It is the last running total, everyone counted so far.
steps.say: These running totals are the cumulative frequency: each one counts everyone so far. Look at the numbers, no graph needed.
The middle customer is halfway through the 20, and that halfway point marks the median time. To find its position, halve the total.

That is the whole idea. A cumulative frequency graph plots these running totals so you can read across from the halfway height (\(n/2\)) to the median, and from \(n/4\) and \(3n/4\) to the quartiles. A box plot draws those key values, and a histogram handles the same grouped data using frequency density.
